optionRationales.C: Supply-chain controls like signing address model/artifact provenance, not the trustworthiness of documents surfaced by retrieval at runtime.
optionRationales.D: Internal storage does not make content trustworthy once it can be edited by an attacker; retrieved chunks must always be treated as untrusted input regardless of source.

questions.topic: Improper output handling (LLM05) — treating model output as untrusted
questions.question:
An internal tool takes an LLM's generated response and inserts it directly into a web page's HTML and into a downstream SQL query, with no encoding, escaping, or validation, because "the model is trusted." A crafted prompt causes the model to emit content that executes as script in the browser.
Which risk category does this map to, and what is the correct fix?

options.A: LLM05 Improper Output Handling; encode/validate the model's output before it is rendered in HTML or used in a query, the same as any other untrusted input
options.B: LLM06 Excessive Agency; restrict the agent's tool scopes so it cannot call the rendering function
options.C: This is not a security issue, since the content originated from the organization's own model rather than from a user
options.D: Improve the system prompt so the model is instructed never to output unsafe HTML or SQL

questions.rationale: This is Improper Output Handling (LLM05): model output must be treated as untrusted, the same as any other input, and encoded/validated before use in a sensitive downstream context like HTML rendering or a SQL query.

optionRationales.A: Correct. LLM05 applies whenever generated output is consumed downstream without treating it as untrusted; encoding/validation before HTML render or query use is the fix.
optionRationales.B: Excessive Agency concerns how much autonomous action an agent can take with tools, not how raw text output is encoded before being rendered or queried.
optionRationales.C: Output originating from the model is still attacker-influenceable via the prompt, so it must be treated as untrusted before downstream use.
optionRationales.D: A system-prompt instruction is not an enforceable technical control; it does not reliably prevent unsafe content from reaching an unguarded rendering or query path.

questions.topic: MCP/agent hardening — least-privilege tool scopes
questions.question:
An agent connected to an MCP server for a ticketing system has been granted the full admin API scope, even though the agent only ever needs to create read-only summary reports.
What is the correct hardening step?

options.A: Narrow the agent's tool scope to only the specific report-creation/read action it needs, instead of the full admin scope
options.B: Add a system-prompt instruction telling the agent not to misuse its admin access
options.C: Route the agent's text output through Llama Guard before it is shown to the user
options.D: Embed a long-lived admin API key directly in the agent's tool configuration for reliability

questions.rationale: Least-privilege tool scopes mean granting an agent only the specific actions it needs; an admin-scoped credential for a read-only reporting task is an unnecessary excess-privilege exposure that should be scoped down.

optionRationales.A: Correct. Least-privilege scoping means granting only the specific action(s) the agent actually needs, not a broad admin scope.
optionRationales.B: A prompt instruction is not an enforceable security boundary; it does not prevent misuse if the underlying credential still has full admin power.
optionRationales.C: Llama Guard screens content for safety categories; it does not constrain what API scope or permissions a tool credential holds.
optionRationales.D: This is the opposite of correct practice — hardening calls for identity-based auth with no static, long-lived secrets, not embedding one for convenience.

questions.topic: MCP/agent hardening — policy broker authorizing tool calls
questions.question:
In an agent's current architecture, when the model decides to invoke an MCP tool, the call is sent straight to the backend system and executes immediately, with no intermediate check — including for destructive actions such as deleting records.
What control is missing?

options.A: A policy broker/gateway that authorizes each tool call, evaluating the specific action and arguments, before it is allowed to execute
options.B: A lower model sampling temperature, so the model selects tools more conservatively
options.C: A cap on the number of tool calls allowed per session
options.D: After-the-fact logging of every tool call for later audit review

questions.rationale: MCP/agent hardening calls for a policy broker or gateway that authorizes each individual tool call before execution — this is the preventive control missing here, especially for destructive actions.

optionRationales.A: Correct. A policy broker/gateway authorizing each tool call before execution is exactly the preventive control missing from this architecture.
optionRationales.B: Sampling temperature affects text generation randomness; it provides no enforceable authorization boundary over which tool calls are allowed to execute.
optionRationales.C: A per-session call cap addresses volume/overuse concerns, not whether any individual destructive call is authorized before it runs.
optionRationales.D: Logging after execution is detective, not preventive — it does not stop a damaging action, such as a deletion, from having already happened.

questions.topic: MCP/agent hardening — untrusted tool arguments (Excessive Agency, LLM06)
questions.question:
An agent with file-system access calls a delete_file tool. The file-path argument is generated by the model itself from the conversation. A crafted user prompt causes the model to pass a path pointing outside the intended sandbox directory.
What is the correct control to prevent this?

options.A: Allowlist-validate tool arguments derived from model output (e.g., restrict the path to an approved directory) before the call executes
options.B: Trust the argument as-is, since it was produced by the model's own reasoning about the user's request
options.C: Disable logging for delete operations to reduce noise in the audit trail
options.D: Increase the model's context window so it has more information available when deciding on the path

questions.rationale: Any tool argument derived from model output must be treated as untrusted and allowlist-validated before execution; this directly mitigates Excessive Agency (LLM06), where a loosely-scoped agent action can be steered outside its intended bounds.

optionRationales.A: Correct. Allowlist-validating model-derived arguments (e.g., restricting the path to an approved directory) before execution is the control that prevents this specific path-traversal-style abuse.
optionRationales.B: Model output, including arguments it generates, is influenceable by the prompt and must be treated as untrusted, not implicitly trusted because the model produced it.
optionRationales.C: Removing logging reduces the ability to detect or investigate the abuse; it does nothing to prevent it and contradicts good practice.
optionRationales.D: A larger context window does not add a validation or authorization boundary around what arguments a tool call may execute with.

questions.topic: Detection engineering over model I/O telemetry + Google SAIF
questions.question:
A security team wants to build detection rules to catch attacks such as prompt-injection attempts and unusual agent behavior in a production LLM application, and wants an overarching framework to organize this alongside their other AI security controls.
Which approach is soundest?

options.A: Build detection rules over combined input, retrieval, and output telemetry to flag anomalies (e.g., repeated injection patterns, unusual tool-call arguments), organized under a framework such as Google SAIF
options.B: Rely solely on the model's own self-reported confidence score as the detection signal
options.C: Stop logging retrieval-stage data to cut storage costs, since only the final output matters for detection
options.D: Skip detection engineering entirely, since Prompt Guard already blocks all injection attempts at ingestion

questions.rationale: Sound detection engineering builds rules over model I/O telemetry across input, retrieval, and output stages, and Google SAIF is an overarching practitioner framework for organizing AI security controls like this one alongside guardrails and hardened tool surfaces.

optionRationales.A: Correct. Detection rules over input/retrieval/output telemetry, organized under an overarching framework such as Google SAIF, is the sound approach described in guidance.
optionRationales.B: A model's self-reported confidence is not a verified or independent detection signal and is not a documented substitute for telemetry-based detection.
optionRationales.C: Dropping retrieval-stage logging removes exactly the data needed to trace indirect-injection or poisoning incidents back to the offending chunk.
optionRationales.D: No single classifier is a complete prevention guarantee; detection/monitoring remains a necessary defense-in-depth layer even alongside a guardrail like Prompt Guard.
